en: Majjhima Nikāya 119, Kāyagatāsati Sutta:
Mindfulness Directed to the Body.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, after the meal, on returning from their alms round, a large number of bhikkhus assembled and sat together in the assembly hall, and this discussion arose among them:
“It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends!”

"To such an extent has mindfulness directed to the body been declared by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—to be developed and cultivated so as to be of great fruit and great benefit.

Now, while this conversation among those bhikkhus was still unfinished, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion in the evening and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?
“Venerable sir, just now, after we had returned from our alms round following the meal, we were sitting together and assembled in the assembly hall when this conversation arose among us:”
“It is wonderful, friend! It is marvelous, friend!

To such an extent has mindfulness directed to the body been declared by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—to be of great fruit and great benefit when developed and cultivated.
“This was our conversation, Bhante, which remained unfinished, when the Blessed One arrived.”
“And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down. Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, he breathes in mindful and breathes out mindful.
Breathing in long, he knows, “I am breathing in long”; breathing out long, he knows, “I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, he knows, “I am breathing in short”; breathing out short, he knows, “I am breathing out short.
He trains himself, “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body”; he trains himself, “I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.”
He trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.
As he dwells thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled internally, stilled, unified, and concentrated.
In this way, monks, a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body.

Furthermore, monks, when walking, a monk understands: "I am walking"; when standing, he understands: "I am standing"; when sitting, he understands: "I am sitting"; when lying down, he understands: "I am lying down.
Or, in whatever manner his body is disposed, he understands it accordingly.
As he dwells thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within himself.
It is in this way, monks, that a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; and he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
He acts with clear comprehension; he acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
As he dwells thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within himself.
In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the hair of the head, enclosed by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;..."
"The heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, bile,
phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine. Monks,
it is just as if there were a two-mouthed sack full of various kinds of grain, such as this:
Of rice, paddy, mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and husked rice— a man with good eyesight, having released it, would examine it:
"This is rice, this is paddy, these are mung beans, these are black gram, these are sesame seeds, these are husked rice."
In the same way, monks, a monk contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upward and from the hair of the head downward, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews,
bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, excrement, bile..."
“Phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.
As he dwells thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, those memories and intentions associated with the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled within himself; it becomes stilled, unified, and concentrated.
In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, in terms of its elements:
"In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element."
“Just as if, monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow and divided it into portions, were sitting at a crossroads;
even so, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, according to its elements:
‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’”
As he dwells thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled, composed, unified, and concentrated within himself.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, dead for one day, or two days, or three days—swollen, discolored, and festering.
He compares this very body with it:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."
As he dwells thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled inwardly; it becomes stilled, unified, and concentrated.
In this way too, monks, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground,
being devoured by crows, or being devoured by hawks, or being devoured by vultures,
or being devoured by herons, or being devoured by dogs, or being devoured by tigers, or being devoured by leopards.
Or being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of worms.
He applies this to his own body:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."
As he is thus diligent … [as before] … in this way too,
bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body. Furthermore, bhikkhus,

suppose a bhikkhu were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, bound together by sinews … [as before] … In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
A skeleton, fleshless and smeared with blood, bound together by sinews; ...
a skeleton, devoid of flesh and blood, bound together by sinews; ...
bones detached from their connections, scattered in all directions and intermediate points—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone.
One [bone] for the ankle bone, another for the shin bone, another for the thigh bone,
another for the hip bone, another for the rib bone, another for the spine bone, another for the shoulder blade bone,
another for the neck bone, another for the jaw bone, another for the tooth bone, and another for the skull.
He applies this very same body [as a comparison]:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this state.
As he is thus diligent... [and so on].
In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a bhikkhu were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground—
bones whitened, resembling the color of a conch shell … [and so on] … pe … [as in the full sutta].
He sees bones heaped up, three years old...
bones rotted and crumbled to dust. He applies this same [contemplation] to his own body: "This body, too, is of the same nature, will become like that, and is not exempt from that fate."
‘This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this.
As he is thus diligent...
In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna.

He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“Just as, monks, a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice, having poured bath-powder into a bronze basin,
would sprinkle it repeatedly with water and knead it, so that the ball of bath-powder becomes saturated with moisture,
permeated with moisture, moistened through and through, yet does not drip;”
In the same way, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
As he is thus diligent...
...and so on... In this way too, monks, a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, ... and so on... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna.

Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
Just as, monks, there might be a deep pool of water with its source hidden, which has no inlet of water from the eastern direction, nor from the western direction, nor from the northern direction...
There is no inlet for the water from the southern direction, nor is there an inlet for the water from any other direction;
and though the rain-god should not pour down a proper shower from time to time, yet a cool stream of water would well up from that very lake itself,
so that it would drench, steep, fill, and suffuse that same lake with its cool water.
There would be no part of that entire lake untouched by the cool water;
even so, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration,
so that there is no part of his entire body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
As he dwells thus heedful...
[as before] ...in this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.

Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the fading away as well of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with pleasure devoid of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by pleasure devoid of rapture.
Just as, monks, in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses— some blue, pink, or white lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, and not rising above the water—
Suppose there were a lotus pond, not growing from seeds, whose shoots, from their tips down to their roots,
were completely saturated, drenched, filled, and suffused with cool water, such that there was no part of any of those blue, red, or white lotuses whatsoever that was not touched by the cool water.

In the same way, monks, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the happiness divested of rapture, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that happiness divested of rapture.
As he is thus diligent...
[as before] ...in this way too, monks, a monk develops mindfulness directed to the body.
Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He sits pervading this very body with a pure and bright mind; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
Just as if, monks, a man were sitting covered from head to foot in a white cloth, there would be no part of his entire body unpervaded by that white cloth.
In the same way, monks, a monk sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused by that pure and bright mind.
As he dwells thus—heedful, ardent, and resolute—those memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned.
With their abandonment, his mind becomes settled inwardly, grows calm, becomes unified, and attains concentration.
In this way too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops mindfulness directed to the body.
For anyone, bhikkhus, in whom mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, all wholesome states that partake of true knowledge are included therein.
Just as, bhikkhus, for anyone whose mind is pervaded by the great ocean, all the streams that flow toward the ocean are included therein.
In the same way, monks, for whomever mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, all wholesome states that partake of true knowledge are contained within it.
For whomever, monks, mindfulness directed to the body has not been developed and cultivated, Māra finds an opening, Māra finds an opportunity.
Just as if, monks, a man were to throw a heavy stone ball onto a mound of wet clay.
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
would that heavy stone ball find a way into a mound of wet clay?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“In the same way, monks, for anyone in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been developed and cultivated, Māra finds an opening and Māra finds an opportunity.
It is just as if there were a dry piece of wood, a withered stump,
and a man were to come along carrying a fire-drill, thinking:”
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, monks, would that man, taking that dry, withered piece of wood as an upper fire-stick and rubbing it, produce fire and manifest heat?”
“Yes, Bhante.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, for anyone in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been developed and cultivated, Māra finds an opening, Māra finds an opportunity.
Just as, bhikkhus, a water-jar that is empty and hollow, when placed on its stand, [is easily filled];”
Then suppose a man were to come along carrying a load of water.
What do you think, monks,
would that man be able to set down the water?"
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, for anyone in whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been developed and cultivated, Māra finds an opening; Māra finds an opportunity.
But for anyone in whom mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, Māra does not find an opening; Māra does not find an opportunity.”
“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to throw a light ball of thread against a door-panel made entirely of solid heartwood.
What do you think, bhikkhus,
would that man be able to find an opening for that light ball of thread in the door-panel made entirely of solid heartwood?”
“No, venerable sir.
“In the same way, bhikkhus, for anyone who has developed and cultivated mindfulness directed to the body, Māra finds no opening, and Māra finds no foothold.
Just as with a piece of wet, sap-filled wood;”
Then suppose a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, monks?
“Would that man, by taking that moist, sap-filled piece of wood as an upper fire-stick and rubbing it, produce fire and manifest heat?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“In the same way, monks, for anyone in whom mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, Māra finds no opening, and Māra finds no foothold.”
“Suppose, monks, there were a water jar full of water, brimming to the top so that a crow could drink from it, set upon a stand;
then a man would come along carrying a load of water.
What do you think, monks?”
“Would that man be able to find a place to pour out the water?”—
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”—
“In the same way, monks, for anyone who has developed and cultivated mindfulness directed to the body, Māra finds no opening, and Māra finds no foothold.”
“Monks, whoever has developed and cultivated mindfulness directed to the body is capable of realizing,
to whatever extent he directs his mind toward it, any state that is to be realized through direct knowledge,
provided there is a suitable basis for such realization.”
“Monks, suppose there were a water-jar, full of water, brimful so that a crow could drink from it, set upon a stand.
If a strong man were to pull at it from this side or that, would water come out?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“In the same way, bhikkhus, for anyone by whom mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated,
whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he inclines his mind toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge,
he attains the capacity to be a witness therein, in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a square pond on level ground, with embankments, full of water, brimming so that a crow could drink from it.
If a strong man were to release the embankment from this side or that, would the water come out?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“In the same way, monks, for anyone who has developed and cultivated mindfulness directed to the body,
whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he inclines his mind toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge,
he attains the capability of being a witness therein, in each and every case where there is a suitable basis.”
“Bhikkhus, just as if there were a chariot on level ground at a crossroads, harnessed to thoroughbreds, standing with its pole raised and its goad ready,

and a skilled trainer, a master of taming horses, having mounted it, took the reins in his left hand and the goad in his right hand, and could drive it wherever he wished, whether forward or backward— even so, bhikkhus,
for anyone by whom mindfulness directed to the body has been developed and cultivated, whatever [goal] he may have...”
He inclines his mind toward the realization of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge;
he attains the capacity for realization in each respective sphere whenever there is a suitable occasion.

Monks, when mindfulness directed to the body has been practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken, these ten benefits are to be expected.
He is one who endures both the unpleasant and the pleasant; he is not overcome by the unpleasant, but dwells having mastered any unpleasantness that has arisen.
He is one who endures fear and terror; he is not overcome by fear and terror, but dwells having mastered any fear and terror that have arisen.
He is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
He is one who is accustomed to patiently enduring harsh and offensive verbal attacks, as well as arisen bodily feelings that are painful,
sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening. He is one who gains at will,
without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

Thus he experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears... [as far as] he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near...
[as far as] he understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing them with his own mind.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," or a mind free from lust...
[and so on] ...or a mind with hatred...
A mind free from hatred...
a mind with delusion...
or a mind free from delusion...
Whether the mind is contracted … or whether the mind is distracted … or whether the mind is exalted …
...a mind that is not sublime ...
a surpassable mind ...
or an unsurpassable mind ...
...a concentrated mind ...
an unconcentrated mind ...
a liberated mind ...
Or, when the mind is unliberated, he understands, "The mind is unliberated.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.

“With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, remains therein.

Monks, when mindfulness directed to the body has been practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these ten benefits are to be expected.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Those bhikkhus were uplifted and greatly rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body, the ninth, is concluded.
